study_identification_part.si4_title: A generalizable normative deep autoencoder for brain morphological anomaly detection: application to the multi-site StratiBip dataset on bipolar disorder in an external validation framework

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop a generalizable multivariate normative modelling framework based on deep autoencoders for characterizing brain morphology in bipolar disorder, integrated with a confounder removal step that enables external validation across multi-site datasets.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: The paper provides detailed description of M-ComBat harmonization. The HCP-YA was used as reference site. The external StratiBip test set HC portion (N=363) was concatenated with HCP-YA training set to estimate site effects, which were then applied to harmonize all test data (both HC and BD). Age, sex, and TIV were preserved as biological covariates. Comprehensive validation was performed including statistical tests, SVM classification, and biological covariate preservation checks. The harmonization was specifically designed for external validation framework. M-ComBat harmonization method; batch variable = site (7 StratiBip sites harmonized to HCP-YA reference); covariates preserved = age, sex, TIV (for volume features); external test set HC portion used to estimate site effects with reference training set; harmonization validated through: (1) Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA comparing feature distributions across sites pre/post harmonization, (2) SVM site classification showing decreased performance post-harmonization (f1-score from 95% to 23%), (3) preservation of biological covariates assessed via linear regression models; out-of-sample harmonization framework for external validation

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Multiple metrics: (1) Mean deviation scores (MDS) based on mean squared error (MSE) averaged across all 170 features; (2) Feature-specific reconstruction errors (RE); (3) Modified z-scores (mZ) using median and median absolute deviation (MAD) for individual-level assessment; (4) Abnormality threshold: feature-specific 99th percentile of normative RE distribution; (5) Mean extreme values (MEV): 99% trimmed mean (top 1% extreme values)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper describes multiple deviation metrics in detail. Subject-level MDS is computed by averaging squared reconstruction errors across all features. Feature-specific REs are calculated as squared errors between original and reconstructed instances. For individual-level inference, modified z-scores (mZ) are computed using the median and MAD of the normative RE distribution. Abnormality is defined using feature-specific 99th percentile thresholds from the normative distribution. For extreme value analysis, the mean of the top 1% extreme values (99% trimmed mean) is used.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: From the reconstructed StratiBip data, for each feature, we extracted the RE, the squared error between the original and reconstructed instances, REvj = ( xvj − x̂vj ) 2 . Then, the RE values were integrated with the MSE for computing the subject ' s mean deviation scores (MDS) by averaging the squared error across all the features : MDSJ = ∑ V v ( xvj − x̂vj ) 2 V... Then, the mZ score foresees that each new data point be standardized with the median and MAD of the normative expected RE distribution... we defined a threshold for each feature based on its specific normative RE distribution... For each normative RE feature distribution, we took the mZ threshold corresponding to the 99th percentile... we applied a block maxima approach, where a series of independent observations are summarized by its maximum value within a specific block... the top 1 % mean of extreme values (MEV), i.e., the 99 % trimmed mean

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-level analyses: (1) Mann-Whitney U (MWU) one-tailed tests comparing feature-specific RE distributions between BD and HC groups, with cliff's delta effect size and bootstrap 95% CI for p-values (uncorrected p<0.05) to identify BD-deviating features; (2) Two-tailed MWU mass-univariate analysis on corrected features with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons; (3) ROC curve analysis for BD vs HC discrimination using MDS, with AUC and optimal threshold identification. Heterogeneity analyses: Pairwise RE absolute differences within and between groups to compute mean heterogeneity. Extreme value analyses: Block maxima approach comparing mean extreme values (top 1%, 99% trimmed mean) across groups using leave-one-out CV. Individual-level analyses: Modified z-scores for personalized brain deviating maps; feature-specific abnormality frequencies; pairwise overlap coefficient and Jaccard similarity to assess spatial overlap of abnormal maps within and between groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: BD group showed significantly higher brain deviations than HC (median MDS difference: -0.0276), greater heterogeneity in deviations, and more extreme values, with deviations prominently in basal ganglia, hippocampus, and adjacent regions; however, individual-level abnormalities showed greater spatial overlap between BD and HC than within BD group, suggesting BD alterations are heterogeneous and partly nested within healthy variation.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The autoencoder-based normative model achieved training MSE of 0.182 (95% CI: 0.179-0.185) and validation MSE of 0.222 (95% CI: 0.211-0.233). BD group showed significantly higher median MDS (0.2264, 95% CI: 0.2210-0.2324) compared to HC (0.1988, 95% CI: 0.1945-0.2030), with median difference of -0.0276 (95% CI: -0.0339 to -0.0216). Feature-specific analyses identified significantly higher BD deviations in: right inferior temporal gyrus CT, and volumes of striatum, CA4, CA2_3, anterior cerebellum, and adjacent to globus pallidus (cliff's delta effect sizes ranging from -0.10 to -0.13). In mass-univariate comparison, only WMV adjacent to left globus pallidus survived FDR correction. RE heterogeneity was higher in BD (max mean pairwise difference 1.8±6.8) than HC (0.59±1.2), particularly for WMV of bilateral stratum (ranking 1st and 2nd in BD heterogeneity). Extreme value analysis showed BD had more pronounced extreme deviations, with 15 features showing at least double MEV compared to normative and HC groups (including 7 CT, 4 GMV, 4 WMV features). MDS-based BD vs HC discrimination achieved AUC-ROC of 0.6129 (95% CI: 0.5989-0.6270) with accuracy of 58.3%, improving slightly to AUC 0.6218 and accuracy 59.0% when using extreme values. Individual-level analyses showed BD subjects had 1.9% abnormal features on average (≈3 features/subject) compared to 1.3% in HC (≈2 features/subject). The highest abnormality frequencies were found in WMV adjacent to left globus pallidus (11.0% in BD, 6.9% in HC) and GMV of right thalamus (7.5% in BD, 6.3% in HC). Spatial overlap analysis revealed HC group had higher similarity (overlap coefficient: 0.72; Jaccard: 0.32) than BD (overlap coefficient: 0.60; Jaccard: 0.23), and notably, inter-group BD-HC overlap (0.67; 0.27) was higher than within-BD overlap, suggesting heterogeneity in BD and potential nesting of BD alterations within healthy variation.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The paper acknowledges several limitations: (1) medication effects not controlled in BD group, so group differences may partly reflect medication rather than disorder-specific effects; (2) comorbidities not accounted for; (3) ComBat and linear regression may not fully capture non-linear confounding effects; (4) uncertainty in MRI-based features from CAT12 segmentation, particularly for subcortical regions with reduced GM-WM contrast; (5) autoencoder lacks directionality information (cannot determine if deviation is too high or too low); (6) difficulty evaluating false-positive deviations without ground truth; (7) incomplete lifespan assessment (only young adults 22-37 years); (8) sample size and biological covariates not equally distributed among sites; (9) ROI-level rather than voxel-level analysis reduces spatial granularity; (10) does not address underlying aetiology of psychiatric disorders, operating in unsupervised framework accepting unknown aetiology; (11) limited clinical applicability without mapping to treatment outcomes or behavioral profiles.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: the data was not corrected for medication on BD, therefore we cannot exclude the possibility that the significant group differences and brain deviations may be driven by medication effects. Similarly, we did not account for comorbidities which might be important to distinguish between disorder-specific effects and others... linear regression, despite its simplicity and ease of implementation, might not fully capture the biological effects if these encompass non-linearities... CAT12 brain tissue segmentation is based on algorithms that may encounter challenges in segmenting small brain regions with mixed tissues... the RE lacks information about directionality... The absence of a ground truth for brain deviations limits the ability to distinguish true abnormalities from spurious findings... there was an incomplete assessment of BD across the entire lifespan, as the dataset only included young adults... ROI-based analysis was employed instead of utilizing all voxel-based whole-brain data... a major challenge for a potential clinical application is that our approach does not directly address the issue of understanding the underlying aetiology of psychiatric disorders

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study implemented several notable innovations: (1) First multivariate normative framework integrating three modalities (CT, GMV, WMV) simultaneously; (2) Novel confounder removal pipeline generalizable to external datasets, combining M-ComBat harmonization with biological covariate regression in external validation framework; (3) Comprehensive heterogeneity assessment including pairwise RE differences and extreme value statistics (block maxima with 99% trimmed mean); (4) Modified z-scores using median and MAD for robust individual-level inference; (5) Feature-specific abnormality thresholds based on 99th percentile of normative distribution; (6) Spatial overlap analysis using both overlap coefficient and Jaccard similarity; (7) Custom neurocombat_pyClasse implementation compatible with sklearn Pipelines; (8) Bootstrap validation with 1000 iterations to assess model robustness; (9) Code and trained model made publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/inesws/Normative_AE.git) with demo test code.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a methodologically rigorous study demonstrating external validation of a deep learning normative model across multiple sites. Key strengths include the comprehensive confounder removal pipeline, extensive validation of harmonization effectiveness, and multi-level analysis framework (group-level, heterogeneity, extreme values, and individual-level). The study is notable for being the first to apply multivariate autoencoder-based normative modeling to bipolar disorder with simultaneous integration of cortical thickness, gray matter, and white matter volumes. The finding that BD abnormalities show greater overlap with HC than within BD group itself provides important evidence for the heterogeneity hypothesis in psychiatric disorders. The authors appropriately note that ROI estimates for white matter in gray matter regions (and vice versa) reflect volumes adjacent to those regions due to CAT12's tissue segmentation approach. Training data from HCP-YA is publicly available; StratiBip data is not publicly available due to data-use agreements. The study was supported by multiple European and international funding agencies including EBRAINS-Italy, Italian Ministry of Health and Research, Pittsburgh Foundation, and CIHR. First author Sampaio was supported by EBRAINS-Italy NextGenerationEU funding.
